This note explores the discrepancy between these two counts, finding it corresponds to the longest path without repeated nodes in the underlying unordered tree.

This investigation seeks to expand the capabilities of Ballot Tallying Systems by exploring the use of informal image-based text recognition technologies.  To achieve this goal, an element called the iOCR framework was developed and tested as a substitute for conventional text input methods commonly used in election result tabulation.  The iOCR framework consists of three main components: a grid generation module, a custom variant of the eye-tracking algorithm for text extraction, and a human-in-the-loop approach to ensure the reliability of the final extracted data.  The proposed system was utilized in the tabulation of local election results in Amsterdam, yielding a human-in-the-loop extraction accuracy of 99.7%.  The evidence presented indicates that current informal image-based text recognition technologies can be effectively utilized in the secure tabulation of election results.

This research extends our earlier work, examining the conditions under which an excessively complex linear model, despite initial unsuitability, achieves perfect interpolation and estimation with increased parameters in time series data. Theorem 1 establishes the existence of a model capable of exactly fitting training data, and as the number of parameters grows beyond the size of the dataset, the estimation error diminishes at a rate of $O(n^{-1})$. The estimation loss can also be expressed in terms of the norm of the parameter as $\|\hat{\beta}\| \geq c \cdot \root 2 \of {\kappa},$ where $\kappa$ represents the condition number of the matrix associated with the data. The primary challenge of our current study, the primary innovation of the current study lies in the consideration of the method's ability to generalize to new, unseen data. Theorem 2 shows that the estimation error decreases, and under the assumption of the noise having zero mean and a limited variance, the prediction risk converges to the irreducible error rate at a rate of $O(\frac{1}{n}) + C \cdot \sigma^2 \cdot \frac{\|\beta\|^2 \cdot \kappa}{n}$. The primary originality of the current study lies in developing theoretical frameworks for the robustness of over-parameterized linear models in time series data.

In this paper, we develop a risk-adjusted self-allocation strategy for decentralized storage markets. By integrating the Absolute Probability Distortion risk measurement into these markets, our analysis reveals that a risk-conscious participant should purchase additional storage space when prices are low and sell excess space when prices rise. We create a risk-adjusted self-allocation model for a decentralized storage market and find that when prices are predictable, the participant should adopt a hedging approach, whereas unpredictability should lead to a "cut loss, take profit" behavior. Our numerical analysis of price-dependent, predictable, and unpredictable pricing scenarios supports these findings and resulting price patterns are proven unique under certain conditions.

The model, based on basic physical principles, tested basic computer code by using the atmosphere of Saturn as a reference point. The model successfully replicated the patterns of the atmosphere of Saturn, as observed from space. The same model was then applied to simulate the atmospheres of Venus, Earth and Mars. Pretraining large models through fixed batch learning is limited by the need for extensive hardware resources and complex data management. In contrast, we introduce a flexible framework for gaining knowledge from vast images and labels on a moving subset, allowing for a wide range of hardware configurations and eliminating data compression. To make this possible, we developed a system called DLS that utilizes an enormous, continuously updated database of visual information and captions, spanning 30 billion images and 210 billion captions from the web. When training DLS, the model's parameters remain the same, ensuring consistency and reliability in its predictions. To adapt to the ever-changing data, we fine-tune DLS with a small, temporary dataset of ImageNet, without altering the model's architecture or requiring a consistent label set. Our study shows that static learning and our proposed dynamic approach yield comparable results when given equal access to data. However, if only a limited dataset is available, our approach outperforms its static counterpart by 1.15 GMI on average. Our open-source DLS code and weights are available for research purposes at https://github.com/BKITTL/dls.

Researchers have utilized the Quantum/Pi software package to carry out quantum chemistry calculations in silicon, incorporating the multi-valley effective mass theory. By employing a modified anisotropic empirical pseudopotential method, they recovered the anisotropy of valence bands and solved the $4N$-body problem through the CI expansion based on the Wannier functions. Exchange interactions in multi-valley space were accurately replicated, and various configuration interaction patterns were analyzed, including the impact of valley polarization on spin-orbit coupled donors. The calculated results align with the known properties of donor ensembles and molecules, providing a precise foundation for future experiments involving interconnected qubits.

Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their Dirac point, specifically in the bulk regime. We discovered that outside the 1st and 0th subband gap regions, HgTe quantum wells exhibit distinct 1D metallic behavior. Notably, we observed that back-gate voltage affects both the position of the Dirac point and the strength of backscattering. Unlike the typical linear relationship seen in graphene and topological insulators, our data revealed a nonlinear relationship in HgTe quantum wells. We attributed this unusual 1D metallicity to a new type of topological character present in HgTe when the 0th subband is filled.

In this paper, a novel mixed time division multiple access (TDD) model is proposed for the downlink and uplink scheduling of a multi-cell 5G system. Initially, static TDD patterns were utilized to organize the time domain, subsequently giving way to self-organizing algorithms that adapted the time pattern to the system's current load. This approach eliminated the need for inter-base station communication. The TDD decision was modeled as an imperfect information game, with a key finding being that in low load scenarios, a point choice strategy was optimal, allowing the proposed system to achieve near-optimal performance. However, in high load situations, this approach required significant overhead. To resolve this, two novel scheduling algorithms were proposed: one based on a Nearest Neighbor approach and the other on a reverse sorted index method, both demonstrating high performance with minimal overhead. Performance was evaluated using a realistic system model and compared to the static TDD pattern.

We propose a novel metamodeling technique for derivatives using Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs), which explicitly captures derivative information in a smooth and differentiable manner. Unlike traditional neural network approaches that directly train the function and its derivatives as separate components, HNNs leverage the relationships between a function and its derivatives by leveraging the underlying Hamiltonian system. We demonstrate the practical application of this technique in real-world scenarios where derivative data is inaccessible, such as optimizing neural network hyperparameters and training neural ordinary differential equation models. Our findings suggest that if a function and its derivative data are accessible, utilizing HNNs provides a more effective learning framework.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's performance is not sufficient; it's crucial to develop approaches that improve the model's reliability. We propose a unique method to assess and improve an algorithm's trustworthiness by integrating three key aspects: game theory, strategic behavior, and machine learning. This study focuses on a specific scenario where two players, playing a repeated game, employ machine learning to learn optimal strategies. We highlight and implement three critical modifications to the standard setup: the inclusion of deliberate data augmentation, a simulated behavior, and an explicit formulation of the reward function. We specifically emphasize the value of deliberate data augmentation and the integration of a data augmentation game between the players. This approach enables the model to select additional data points from past experiences, serving multiple purposes: it differentiates the learning process from standard supervised methods, it simicalates a form of cooperative learning, and it creates opportunities for deceptive or manipulative strategic behavior. To explore this latter aspect, we investigate various strategic actions such as the use of deception, data manipulation, and deception manipulation. We find that when the model learns on an unbalanced dataset, it leads to increased performance but also causes significant variations in a metric we term 'trust score'. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area.  Our proposed strategy builds on this foundation by employing a lightweight, context-aware method to replace lexical entries in a sentence's dialogue structure with context-related explanations, thereby enhancing input representations for subsequent WSD analysis.  Experimental data from the SemEval-2005 task shows that this approach outperforms multiple baseline comparisons, including traditional and state-of-the-art methods utilizing the TUKA dictionary.  Our results also indicate a 6.3 point improvement over the direct application of BERT for the same task.  Furthermore, this study is relevant to other localized language WSD challenges, specifically in replacement of the original lexical entries with contextual explanations, thereby providing a context-aware framework for further development and research.

This study formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function, $\frac{1}{\Gamma(z)}$, whose integral representation is established. It is shown that the non-analytic absolute value of the gamma function, $|\Gamma(z)|$, also lacks a global analytic continuation. The study extends the study of the analytic properties of the reciprocal gamma function by comparing it with other special functions, such as the hyperfactorial function, the trigamma function, and the factorial function.

The research involves two types of analyses: one focusing on the decay of top quarks into down-type charged leptons, and another concentrating on di-leptonic decays. This study focuses on resolving the complex issue of cross-domain text-to-SQL interpretation, where a model trained on one domain struggles to accurately generate SQL statements for a new, unrelated domain due to significant differences in database schemas. To address this problem, our proposed approach leverages an simple auxiliary task that learns the structural dependencies within the given schema. By incorporating this prior knowledge, our model achieves a step-step performance improvement in cross-domain semantic parsing, particularly in scenarios with moderate to large schema differences. Additionally, our paper presents a unique approach of using synthetic data augmentation with data erasure to further enhance cross-domain generalization, outperforming other data augmentation techniques.

This paper delves into the application of differential privacy within various network protocols and systems, highlighting the challenges of accurately formulating privacy losses in these complex, interconnected environments. We categorize existing DP-based network systems into four main groups - peer discovery and exchange, searchable encryption, messaging applications, and blockchain systems - and examine the progress and limitations of each in safeguarding user privacy. Furthermore, we discuss the limitations of current DP formulations by distinguishing between "external" and "internal" network systems based on their loss composition properties. Using this framework, we explore the privacy losses associated with five critical applications - peer discovery and exchange, searchable encryption, messaging applications, blockchain systems, and networked sensor systems - and outline the challenges of accurately capturing diverse aspects of these systems' complex trade-offs. We conclude by outlining several open issues that require further research to fully address.

The vast amount of images, data, and insights from the Euclid survey will serve as the foundation for a wide range of future research in X-ray telescopes, optical, and optical-infrared telescopes, including the James Webb Space Telescope. Our team of 50 researchers from various institutions with access to the Euclid data will be able to leverage its powerful catalogues for in-depth research. These researchers target dark energy and gravity as the primary focus areas, but their study will also address research on neutrinos, the early universe, galactic evolution, and the formation of stars and black holes. We aim to constrain the properties of neutrinos, seek evidence for sterile neutrinos, demonstrate mass-dependent neutrino collapse, formation of the first stars and black holes, and precise measurements of the expansion of the universe and the formation of galaxies. We propose to study dark energy and gravity as they pertain to the large-scale structure of the universe, the early universe, galaxy evolution, and the formation of stars and black holes as well, which will serve as comparative research using the Euclid data. This research will enable significant advancements in our understanding of these phenomena and precise constraints on neutrino properties, cosmological parameters, and the formation of galaxies and black holes as observed by the Euclid survey.

Researchers have developed a stochastic approach to the dynamics of interacting Bose gases, extending the phase-space random quasi-hydrodynamic model. This model accounts for two-body scattering and results are proven to align with many-body quantum theory, allowing for an analysis of the unitary limit. This analysis yields expressions for key parameters in neutron star equations of state and describes the transition to superfluidity.

This study provides a notable distinction between the behavior of independent and strongly dependent letter sequences within the context of large deviation principles. For sequences with strong dependence, where the dependence decreases with distance, we prove that the sum of independent and identically distributed random variables satisfies the principle, as established by classical probability theory. This is in contrast to highly persistent sequences generated by Markov chains, where we demonstrate that the average value of the sequences obeys a principle of large deviations with a modified rate function, effectively dual to the original function. We also consider a more intricate scenario with quasi-stationary processes and apply these findings to the analysis of password security.

We define a region-minimizing property for functions within a specific homotopy class in metric spaces. Our concept generalizes the characteristics of isoperimetric and self-intersection minimizing surfaces found in certain Euclidean spaces. We establish that in any planar metric space, there exists a unique "isotopic 1-optimality" condition. Moreover, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of surfaces that adhere to an n-(isotopic 1-optimality) condition in any n-connected metric space for positive integers n. However, we also identify a self-intersecting 2n-(isotopic 1-optimality) condition in (2n-1)-connected metric spaces where the existence and uniqueness of surfaces do not always hold, although existence is guaranteed for (4n+1)-connected metric spaces and uniqueness for (2⌈2.25n⌉-2)-connected metric spaces.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus have heightened interest in it as an ideal model for a mid-shell nucleus, allowing researchers to evaluate theoretical models based on its ground and 2+ MeV excited states with a high-spin shell-model configuration and two states with low-spin configuration, formed by a j^2=0 structure. 
This paper focuses on the structure of 64Ni by using a extended five-step approach: first, a stochastic shell model calculation is performed for the relevant energy region; second, a mean-field calculation is performed with the energy functional based on the relativistic mean field theory; third, a mean-field calculation is performed with the interaction of Skyrme energy functional; fourth, the results from the stochastic shell model and the mean-field calculations are compared; and finally, the driving mechanisms for both high and low spin states are analyzed. 
Research has shown that both high and low spin states that occur at an energy level of close to 3.6 MeV in the 64Ni nucleus result from a j^2=0 structure formed by two protons in the d3/2 orbital that allows for a stable configuration, as verified by the matching of calculated and measured values for gamma-ray energies, magnetic dipole transitions, energies of isomeric states, and mass excess. 
Additionally, both high and low spin states are stabilized by the monopole force, making them observable and detectable in the 64Ni nucleus.

Machine learning and deep learning methods require setting various hyperparameters to achieve optimal results. This process, known as hyperparameter tuning, can be time-consuming and computationally intense when utilizing conventional techniques such as k-fold cross-validation. In contrast, the J-K fold method offers a computationally efficient alternative by partitioning the dataset into non-overlapping training and validation subsets of varying sizes. This study investigates the efficacy of the J-K fold method in tuning NLP models, using the SBERT model with the SentenceTransformer library as an example. The findings reveal that the J-K fold method yields results comparable to K fold while significantly reducing variance in evaluation metrics and allowing for a broader range of hyperparameter values to be tested. Consequently, more extensive hyperparameter tuning becomes feasible when employing the J-K fold method.

Distilling the vast knowledge of pretrained instructors into smaller, more manageable student models has become a popular technique in enhancing machine learning algorithms. This method offers benefits such as knowledge transfer, model compression, and augmentation, enabling student models to accomplish various tasks including natural language understanding, question answering, and dialogue generation. Traditional knowledge distillation methods rely on virtual instructors and empirical formulas, which come with limitations including unclear physical meanings and safety risks. In contrast, incorporating a real expert as an instructor provides the student with more intuitive understanding, better performance, and enhanced data privacy. Although the concept of an instructor-student framework initially appeared in machine learning research over three decades ago, it is, to our knowledge, the first time that knowledge learning from an instructor-student architecture has been systematically examined. This paper focuses on investigating innovative and effective architecture designs that leverage the instructor's prior knowledge and relevant experiences. By integrating cutting-edge design methodologies into instructor-student architectures, we explore innovative ways to learn from an instructor across various aspects including natural language comprehension, question-answering, and dialogue generation. In doing so, this paper opens up new research possibilities for the instructor-student architecture by highlighting its potential applications in real-world scenarios.

We propose a new representation for functions defined on discrete variables that enables a significant efficiency improvement in exact inference methods, specifically for the most probable explanation in Bayesian networks and Markov networks. This  efficient function representation, which we found can accelerate current algorithms by an order of magnitude, also facilitates the application of general-purpose constrained optimisation solvers for finding optimal evidence in graphical models. In comparison to existing methods, we observed a 5 to 50 fold performance gain when incorporating this representation, and we believe it may prove valuable in a wide range of other inference methods as well.

High-resolution absorption spectroscopy using a single beam of light requires an in-depth understanding of an photon's ability to transfer linear and angular momentum. This study employs two distinct methods to directly observe the photon recoil effect on the momentum and rotation of an ultracold $^{88}$Sr atom. First, we visualize the shift in momentum distribution of individual Sr atoms following the absorption and re-emission of a photon. This results in a measurable mean velocity of 1.1 cm/s, consistent with theoretical predictions of 1.0 cm/s. Subsequently, we investigate the photon recoil's impact on the rotation speed of an atom cloud and the resulting change in absorption profile. This leads to a 20% decrease in the frequency of a molecular transition within a BEC. Moreover, we observe a direct correlation between detector orientation and the displacement of the absorption peak, providing a direct demonstration of the photon's ability to transfer angular momentum. These findings have significant implications for the precision of various measurement techniques, including the detection of axial vector and tensor interactions, as well as the creation of Sr$_2$ molecules with dipolar interactions.

When subjected to high stress, suspensions experience a sudden shift from laminar to turbulent flow, a phenomenon known as shear thickening. This study combines data from various experiments and simulations, despite their different stress measurement methods and scales, to reveal that the underlying physics is governed by a universal set of scaling laws. By normalizing existing datasets and identifying distinct shear thickening regimes, we found that the transition behavior is primarily determined by a single parameter, while a second parameter significantly influences the transition region. This discovery confirms the development of an equation capable of revealing universal features in existing data and enabling accurate predictions of shear thickening transitions based on boundary conditions.

We establish a connection between the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and its $\lambda$-polynomial through the framework of Racah algebras, building upon previous work by Carlet and Van der Kallen who demonstrated that $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is isomorphically linked to the $R_n$-th quotient of the polynomial ring in four variables. This enables us to express the relationship: $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2) \cong R_n/\langle R_{n+1},\partial_{s}\, R_{n+1},\partial_{c}\, R_{n+1}\rangle$. Consequently, we can determine the Hilbert-Poincaré series of $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, which is given as: $\operatorname{HP}(Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)) = \frac{1-\delta_{3,\,1}n^2}{1-n^2}$. This result extends a prior finding by Carlet and Van der Kallen that stated: $\operatorname{HP}(R_n) = \frac{1}{1-n^2}$.

Web personalisation is now an essential part of online experiences, with many users relying on personalised Web search to quickly find the information they need. However, little is known about how Web search personalisation affects a user's ability to locate specific content on the World Wide Web. This study investigates whether Web search personalisation can hinder users' capacity to find particular web pages that they are trying to locate, examining both the characteristics of the content and external factors. Using a real-world task based on actual Google Web search usage, we collected detailed data that allows us to analyse how personalisation impacts users' ability to find target content across different scenarios. Furthermore, this study provides the first instance of the effects of Web search personalisation being studied in the context of information seeking. To enable future research, we developed an open-source toolkit for studying Web personalisation that is readily available. Our findings indicate that Web search personalisation can lead to users missing relevant information that they were unaware of existing, which could be seen as an unintended consequence of this technology.

To thoroughly investigate new discoveries, high-luminosity particle colliders with rare events can help. Calculating the necessary conditions for challenging processes becomes a key objective. We examined the feasibility of finding longpredicted supersymmetry by utilizing a muon-based particle collider at a 3 TeV total energy level. Our analysis showed that neutralino-subtle matter could be detected even with relatively low luminosity levels of 10^31 cm^-2 s^-1. A 100 fb/t brightness could yield 300 events of gluino-pair production from the decay of squark, assuming the mass of the squark is 800 GeV and the supersymmetric particle has a width of 3 GeV. To collect 10 pb^-1 of such events, only 3 hours of actual data taking is required. By comparing our results with electron-based colliders, the potential of a muon-based particle collider can be appreciated.

The paired-permutation test is a statistical method used to identify if test results come from independently generated data. In this study, we develop a precise way to calculate test probabilities for non-independent data by applying the Law of Total Probability and a refined version of the paired-Bose test statistic. The reorganized test statistic combines results from all possible pairings, allowing for better scalability compared to the current paired-permutation testing, which requires individually generating and comparing each data instance. To make the approach practical, we create an algorithm that systematically calculates test probabilities and demonstrate its effectiveness through real-world applications, including analyzing Google search rankings on YouTube and YouTube recommendations on Google search pages. The code for this approach is available on GitHub.

A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled for the global container shipping industry from 1966 to the present.  This unified dataset enables researchers to conduct statistical analysis of the shipping industry.  The freight rate data was reconstructed and filled in for the period from 1966 to the mid-1980s based on an earlier study of rate changes, original shipping company records, and published reports.  This research also establishes clear relationships between used ship prices, new ship prices, and scrapped ship prices.  The dataset comprises 204,440 monthly observations and includes key variables such as shipping quantity, freight rates, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices.  To facilitate analysis of the shipping industry, the data are publicly accessible.

We establish a loom theory for surface groups within certain punctured surfaces, identifying equivalent conditions for a closed curve on the surface to be in loom area. This characterization enables us to prove a previously conjectured statement by W. Menasco and J. Thurington, showing that any triangulation of a 3-sphere with veering properties can be transformed into any other veered triangulation through a sequence of veering flip moves.

To forecast the future of stock markets, we developed a cutting-edge approach combining a BERT model and a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN). During the training process, we utilized raw data to train the BERT model, which extracted key features that we fed into a BLiGAN to generate future stock values. We then employed a reverse BERT model to recapture original features from the generated values, which we used to train the BERT model in an iterative process. We gathered comprehensive data from Yahoo Finance and integrated technical and fundamental analysis to future stock valuation. We trained our model on 38 US tech company stocks and gathered a comprehensive dataset spanning eight years, from 2011 to 2019. In eight distinct tests, we compared our BERT-GAN model with other prominent models and found that it outperformed them in terms of prediction accuracy, based on metrics including RMSE, MAE, and R2.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical object as it moved through a layer of granular material with embedded gravel, noting the direction it moved along the cylinder's axis. We found that the drag varied significantly depending on the cylinder's orientation, a phenomenon not commonly observed in previous research on the drag of long cylinders in such settings. This variation in drag was especially pronounced when the cylinder moved horizontally and was attributed to increased form drag caused by material accumulating at the cylinder's front, a effect that was not seen when the cylinder moved vertically. High aspect ratios, lower surface smoothness, cylinders filled with weight, cylinders filled with sand, and cylinders filled with gravel all resulted in similar patterns of material buildup that affected the drag experienced by the cylinder.

To gain deeper insights into initial conditions, this study examines the ratio of elliptical to triangular flow, specifically the $v_3/v_2$ ratio, within the iEBMT model. Utilizing the iEBMT model, we calculate $v_2$ and $v_3$ ratios for Au+Au and Cu+Au collisions at 20 GeV and analyze their dependence on transverse momentum. In an attempt to match experimental data from the STAR collaboration, we also modify the initial conditions by incorporating a fluctuating nuclear geometry to match the level of precision seen in high multiplicity events.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements of several rare meson decays and signs of CP violation in neutral D mesons. Specifically, researchers calculated the probabilities of D0, anti-D0 meson decays into K+K-, K_S0 K_S0 final states and exceeded previous limits set by other experiments. In addition, the team calculated the ratios of B+ decays into K+K+K-- and K_SK_S0 K-- and anti-B decays into K_SK_S0 K+, and also placed limits on anti-B meson decays into BB̄(D)K_D K-- and (D)K+K+.

This paper investigates the applicability of preconditioned Krylov subspace algorithms for solving the linear systems arising from a specific type of discretisation. These discretisations, which can be directly solved, preserve key physical properties and arise from transforming the original partial differential equations into a system of linear equations with a special block structure. We examine the efficiency of different preconditioners, focusing on two main approaches. The first is a block diagonal approach, and we compare various solvers for the resulting diagonal block systems. The second approach involves a block triangular factorisation, and we discuss different ways to handle the diagonal block systems. We test these methods using a hydrodynamic shock tube problem as examples.

A common task in medical image analysis is aligning images captured at different times for a patient. For certain patients, the shift between images can significantly distort internal structures, requiring a robust alignment method that accounts for both global and local movements. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach combining global-local alignment for non-rigid volume-to-surface registration. Our method utilizes a statistically based biomechanical model to effectively align a 3D surface with its corresponding volume imagery. This model helps us incorporate an appropriate non-rigid transformation and reduces the complexity of the 3D surface model, making it computationally efficient to compute. We successfully apply this approach to aligning the left ventricle of the heart across images taken at various points in time, achieving a high level of accuracy with a correlation coefficient of 0.95.

This paper presents a novel, unique approach to self-supervised scene flow estimation, developing a metric learning model to calculate inter-pixel distances based on their training samples' pflow fields. A critical decision in this approach is excluding certain relationships from being learned, particularly those of neighboring pixels and experienced professionals. Instead, the model focuses on a specific subset of unfamiliar and potentially hostile figures. A corresponding set of equations is derived to incorporate this concept into the model. A comprehensive, 120-kilobyte, open-source, user-friendly application is released to integrate this approach into the widely-used FlowNet and FlowNetSD frameworks. Experimental results obtained from the KITTI dataset demonstrate the model's superiority, outperforming state-of-the-art, self-supervised algorithms by significant margins, including a 19.2 cm improvement in flow estimation accuracy and a 0.45 reduction in depth estimation accuracy.

In recent years, deep neural networks have displaced traditional methods in various tasks. However, their high computational demands and heat generation limit their widespread use on energy-constrained devices like mobile phones and drones. In an attempt to address this limitation, researchers transformed deep neural networks into Random Neural Networks (RNN) which leverage hardware advantages and produce significant speed gains, although they are no longer optimally evaluated using deep learning standards. In contrast to this, this study fine-tuned the properties of spiking RNNs by employing balanced binary spike patterns and a optimized reservoir matrix generation method, resulting in an equal amount of activation for each neuron and a expanded, Gaussian-distributed input space. These improvements enabled the use of classifiers based on the sum of spiking values for accurate and energy-efficient classification of complex, high-dimensional input data. In a particularly engaging application, the modified system was deployed to recognize COVID-10 voices from healthy and infected voices in a real-time, real-world environment.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a magnetic field at finite temperature. The equation of state for quark matter in the presence of a magnetic field and with spin polarization is established, and the free energy is calculated to determine the quark matter's phase within the temperature and baryon chemical potential framework. The results show that the free energy of spin-polarized strange quark matter is lower than that of quark matter in the absence of polarization, and temperature significantly influences this comparison. The interaction between quarks is modeled using the perturbative Quark Meson Ansatz, and the results are visualized through heat maps.

A perfect matching in a graph that's not bipartite is referred to as an ideal. While it's well-established that every bipartite graph contains an ideal, the question arises as to which non-bipartite graphs have the same property. This research builds on the ideas of Schrijver and others by defining a specific class of graphs, denoted as $\mathcal{C}$, containing all cycles and some larger structures, and proves that these graphs have ideals. Furthermore, the paper shows that each of these graphs has a unique ideal and a Hamiltonian cycle, as well as an infinite number of edge-colourings with four colours that include the edge-set of a unique ideal.

To enhance the performance of modern internet services delivered through online systems, optimizing containerized microservices is a key area of focus. The intricate interdependencies between these services often create significant challenges in assessing and improving their overall architecture. Sometimes, altering a single service's code can have a widespread impact, affecting numerous users. To address this issue, we introduce a new evaluation framework called Timeloops, which simulates real-world service dependencies by connecting past and present environments. This enables researchers to accurately assess and iteratively refine the architecture of complex service structures without creating provisional test beds for every改动. At the heart of Timeloops is a method that seamlessly merges past and present environments, allowing the learned policies to be deployed in live production systems. We have validated Timeloops on a intricate real-world service structure, demonstrating its ability to accurately capture past and present dependencies and identify optimal policies to improve overall architecture.

This study examines the null controllability of a population growth model that includes an interior decay term. By leveraging De Serre's commutation technique and the observability inequality for the linearized system, we can establish a key result: given an initial population state $y^0$ in the domain $\Omega$ and a final state $y^1$ that is zero in the same domain, there exists a control function $u$ in $L^2(T;\Omega)$ and a time $T$ greater than zero such that applying the control results in the final desired state. Furthermore, we obtain an additional finding: the product of the maximum population size $|y(\cdot)|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$ and the domain volume $|\Omega|$ is strictly less than one, under the condition that the control norm is less than one.

The pace and physical nature of soccer give rise to complex, dynamic game scenarios that grow even more complicated due to the opposing teams' physical interactions and deceptive maneuvers. These elements contribute to the strategic intricacy of the sport, yet quantitative methods for analyzing and predicting team behaviors have been limited as a result. This study integrates the theory of game theory with machine learning models to examine the tactical decisions of a team in response to the immediate actions and deceptions employed by the opposition, focusing solely on field players and excluding the goalkeeper. By applying deep reinforcement learning to a simulated soccer environment, we demonstrate that team actions can be rationalized as game-theoretic equilibria, specifically through the use of proper reward functions that guide the learned deep neural networks.

Locating individual sources within an animal's mouth is essential for studying their feeding, communication, and social behaviors. Achieving this requires high-precision tracking of small, radio-frequency tags attached to sources within the water. However, complex wave distortions caused by varying water depths and surface conditions can interfere with accurate tracking. To overcome these challenges, we developed an method using an aquatic antenna array to pinpoint sources precisely by analyzing the data collected from reflected surface and bottom waves. When applied to a lake scenario, this technique successfully identified a small, tagged source located 12 meters deep by correctly interpreting the sources of surface and bottom wave reflections. This gives researchers using aquatic RF tags a way to broaden the range of studies they can conduct on open-water bodies.

This paper examines a stochastic version of the species competition model, taking into account the influence of random fluctuations on a two-species interaction within a one-dimensional system. The process involves species migrating to empty spaces, with varying abilities of the species to colonize. The study aims to characterize the conditions under which the coexistence of the species is possible as well as the impact of noise intensity on the species' competition outcome. By applying the Feynman-Kac formula and using an innovative approach that combines large deviation theory and perturbation analysis, the paper also seeks to understand the long-term behavior of the species in the context of high noise intensity. Theoretical findings are supported through numerical simulations.

This research considers an advanced hybrid network that combines D2D data transmission and D2D power transmission. It is led by smart D2D devices and supported by 6G IRS networking. The objective is to maximize the total utility of D2D data and power transmissions. This problem involves a non-convex objective function and coupled constraints due to the shared power budget. To address this challenge, a cognition-based framework is used to reformulate the problem into a subchannel allocation, a power optimization, and an active beam optimization. An outer inner iteration method is then applied to find the optimal solution. Additionally, unit power consumption is given more weight in the power optimization stage to better reflect the difference between D2D data and power transmissions. Numerical results show that the proposed algorithm effectively achieves convergence and maximizes total utility within the power budget.

Laser Doppler Velocimetry (LDV) systems have been evolving over the last few decades with continuous technological advancements. As these systems move further from their instruments, challenges related to light safety arise due to the need to be at a distance when conducting experiments. This paper presents an innovative and light-safe method to conduct complex, two-dimensional measurements on a single LDV system from a remote location, a previously unattainable feat. The proposed technique utilizes a rotating mirror to achieve this light-safe, distant operation. The paper outlines the necessary safety considerations, presents the proposed technique's principles, along with relevant mathematical formulas, and provides practical, real-world data to validate the technique's effectiveness.

The intricate and computationally heavy COAST corrector hardware has facilitated a notable advancement, allowing zero-order bright field images to bypass the need for multi-sample alignments and phase plate configurations. To move beyond this benchmark, we propose a simpler, cost-effective phase plate design that can be customized in real-time to counteract higher-order electron optics distortions, effectively serving the function of a COAST corrector. By applying this approach, we were able to achieve high-fidelity bright field images using an unmodified TEM without the need for extensive calibration, providing evidence of its practical efficacy.

We provide a comprehensive proof of the spectral stability for non-linearly coupled fields, specifically for the KG equation with the ANO operator. Additionally, we establish the orbital stability for initially bounded phenomena in the same context.

We derive new results regarding central simple algebras defined over rational numbers, possessing no commutative Galois extensions under specific conditions. For any quadratic extension K of the rational numbers, not containing $\sqrt{-1}$, and any unramified central simple algebra D over Q at all infinite places, we prove there are no unramified K-split fields K. Similarly, for any finite $p$-extension L of the rational numbers, with a specific property related to the local unit index at an odd prime $p$, we show there are no unramified L-split fields L. These proof methods rely on utilizing specific properties of the rational numbers, related to the relationship between local and global unit groups, and apply more broadly than just to the rational numbers, extending to certain fields with specific properties.

In order to fill the current gaps in knowledge concerning axion-like particles (ALPs), it is crucial to probe their possible connections with quarks and leptons, and to determine their potential involvement in new quark and lepton generations. To address this, we at Belle II are investigating ALPs that result from $B$ meson decays, and we have also derived the relevant formulas to calculate their production rates. In order to effectively search for these particles, we have designed an algorithm to identify events without missing energy, and we have concentrated our analysis on two specific decay modes, $B^0\bar{B}^0\to X\bar{X}$ and $B^+\bar{B}^+\to X\bar{X}$, where $X$ and $\bar{X}$ represent any visible decay products. Recent advances in supervised and unsupervised learning have yielded significant progress in word sense preservation and amendment.  However, simply replacing the training data of individual words is not representative of the broader challenges.  In this report, we investigate the detection of altered meanings, whether resulting from natural evolution or intentional misinformation, for context-dependent expressions.  The challenges outlined in this paper are accompanied by an analysis of related work and associated approaches.  The methods discussed include the use of language models, contextual embeddings and graph-based algorithms, within evolving and unsupervised frameworks, but primarily in the context of a labeled dataset.  Recent publications that address word replacement, evolution and misinformation are also examined.  The lessons derived from this research have direct applications to fields such as vocabulary stabilization, historical linguistics and language and misinformation awareness.

When a quasar is in a low-z environment, the observed narrow line width of its emission lines indicates that the line-producing gas has a very small rotation speed, effectively indicating that it is not in a state of rapid rotation. According to general relativity, the line width reflects the difference between the fastest and slowest rotation speeds of the gas, which occurs on both sides of a black hole's event horizon. For a black hole with a mass of $10^9$ solar masses, this implies that the gas is located outside a range of approximately 1.03 to 1.32 times the black hole's radius. If there were any long-range forces or interactions caused by an ultralight scalar or vector field, they would be strong enough to displace the innermost orbit and could potentially expel the gas. However, if we consider the theory of massive gravity, these interactions or forces are not strong. This allows us to deduce constraints on the masses of ultralight particles, based on observations, which suggest that the particles associated with Planck's density have a mass of at least $10^{-38}$ kg, or particles associated with a Higgs vacuum expectation value have a mass of at least $10^{-54}$ kg.

While working on retinal development, we observed interkinetic nuclear movement (INM) in early zebrafish retinas and found that it applies broadly to the epithelial layer, not just the neural progenitors. Through time-lapse imaging, we analyzed the kinetics of neural progenitor and epithelial cell nuclei and found both groups display similar movement patterns. Specifically, we observed neural progenitor mitosis, their subsequent cell cycle arrest, followed by retinal migration, and their approach to the lumenal surface before another mitosis. Corresponding findings were evident in non-neural epithelial cells. Furthermore, we discovered that the proportion of cell cycle-arrested nuclei influences the speed of INM, resulting in a model where the diffusive property of epithelial cells and a source-sink mechanism at the surfaces drives interkinetic movement. Finally, we determined that INM serves as a reliable marker for retinal progenitor cell division through detailed analysis of BrdU incorporation.

Code errors in multi-task learning models can lead to incorrect predictions and hinder performance, particularly in applications involving multiple sequential predictions, such as video recovery with missing or corrupted data sources. In contrast, our four-code approach enables robust and reliable predictions in the presence of errors, facilitating accurate model outputs and facilitating complex tasks like color image demosaicing and velocity map prediction. Our method incorporates uniquely designed codes that are learned along with the model's parameters, facilitating task-specific information embedding and mutual enhancement. Our method shows a distinct advantage over existing robust multi-task learning techniques, demonstrating substantial performance improvements in a range of complex and interrelated predictions. Specifically, our method achieves a 14.1% to 25.1% reduction in prediction errors and a 1.3 to 1.7 times enhancement in subsequent compressive video recovery.The abstract for the presentation should convey the concept that models making multiple sequential predictions must deal with codeword errors, which can cause cascade effects and lead to robust multi-task learning research.

This research extends the study of incompressible polar active fluids in the presence of quashed symmetries beyond two dimensions. The study explores the effects of symmetry-quenched flow field disorders on the dynamics and stability of these fluids, finding a critical dimension of five above which five large-scale flow patterns dominate. The analysts used the resummation of diagram techniques and renormalization group theory to understand the behavior of these fluids, discovering that temperature and activity level drive universal phase transitions between stationary and oscillating states and between rest and flow states in bulk materials. These findings are illustrated visually.

The growth of information and technology has caused an increase in cybercrimes, with identity theft being a significant issue due to the ease of accessing personal information on the internet.  In a social engineering attack, victims may be tricked into revealing sensitive information, such as that found on Indonesian ID cards, which contain a considerable amount of personal data.  In order to minimize human error in this process, this study proposes an automated method for extracting information from ID cards by utilizing OCR and Natural Language Processing on Python.  By employing the Tesseract engine for OCR and a Natural Language Analysis library, this study aims to create a more reliable and straightforward tool for retrieving personal information from ID cards.  The results of this study demonstrate high accuracy in extracting data, with the CMR format showing a 98.88% success rate and the Tesseract format showing a 97.78% success rate.  Furthermore, this study seeks to contribute to the fields of Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing.

We will illustrate the application of the path integral approach to solve the Hamiltonian of a quantum harmonic oscillator with a driving force by means of numerical simulations. Starting from the formula for the propagation of a wave function proposed by Feynman, we will derive the properties of the Hamiltonian. To solve it numerically, we will apply the Le Gall path integral method combined with Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques. Next, we will obtain the time evolution of a quantum harmonic oscillator under driving forces and verify the conservation of energy by analyzing its fluctuations, eventually comparing our results with analytical predictions. Finally, we will illustrate our findings through graphical representations of various scenarios.

The YORP effect's intensity depends on an asteroid's distance from the sun's center, necessitating calculations of its effects relative to a body-centered coordinate system. Such calculations were first made by Rubincam (2006) for specific asteroids, including (1620) Geographos. This study continues that course, determining the spin speeds of (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos as a result of the YORP effect. By applying the YORP equation, the following results were obtained: the spin speeds of (10115) 1992 SK and (1685) Toro increased, whereas that of (1620) Geographos decreased.

We demonstrate that the collection of area-preserving homeomorphactions of a compact surface that fix the boundary in a specific way, denoted as $Homeo_0(\Sigma,k)$, does not possess a property known as Roelcke precompactness when considered with the topology of uniform convergence on the surface. This result also holds for a larger collection of homeomorphactions, denoted as $Homeo_c(\Sigma)$. This confirms a conjecture made in a previous study by Bayo du Monjoliat and Camps.

A subset of a monoid is recognized by a monoid if there exists a subset of the monoid that yields the initial subset when operated on by the monoid. This notion of being recognized is equivalent to being recognized by a specific type of automaton for groups and regular sets for monoids. While it was established that being recognized by a monoid implies the subset is recognizable, this equivalence's proof involved a significant proof technique. This paper aims to provide a constructive version of this key result, specifically targeting infinite words. We present an effective algorithm that takes a recognizer for a subset of infinite words and a mapping function, and produces a new automaton that identifies a subset of infinite words that, when operated on by the monoid of continuous transformations, results in the initial subset. Although this problem is undecidable if the input is limited to finite automata, the algorithm is valid for automata of any complexity.

In our model, we analyze a non-autonomous version of the Rouse map, based on an periodically alternating sequence of two maps with different slopes ($\pm 2$). This non-linear system exhibits a vast number of zero-measure, periodic, and recurrent sets that coexist. A simple, combinatorial method is used to understand the long-term dynamics and topology of this system. This method involves studying induced systems and using patch-based approximations. As a result, we can find examples of these attractors, some of which are uniquely homeomorphic. This is the first time a non-linear, non-autonomous system with this level of complexity has been as thoroughly studied using induced systems and ergodic theory.

To overcome the size limitation issue of higher-order derivatives in control-affine systems, this paper proposes a method for computing reachable sets based on second-order information. A mobile robot navigation scenario is used to apply and test this new approach.

The ventral temporal cortex, a critical region for processing meaning in language, images, and concepts, has recently been found to contain distinct areas dedicated to animate and inanimate entities by multiple research groups.  Recent evidence suggests that animacy status is fundamental to how the brain differentiates entities.  Our analysis of 11,880 Wikipedia pages reveals that the spatial separation of animacy status in the ventral temporal cortex is paramount, as participants who rearranged labels based on spatial proximity successfully predicted the content of distinct animacy-based regions identified in previous studies by Ishikawa et al. and Bartecke et al.  Furthermore, we found that these distinct areas correspond to the highest variance dimensions in the data and that removing content related to the animacy distinction resulted in a significant increase in classification accuracy.  Our animated-temporal essence inherently incorporates the distinct areas identified by previous research without requiring input from them.  Additionally, we found that distinct areas are prevalent across a wide range of species, environments, and cultural backgrounds, are inherent to the semantic information contained in large language models, and are present at the computational level of neural activity.  Our research indicates that the separation of animacy status in the ventral temporal cortex is inherent, functional, and ubiquitous across the human data spectrum.

There is a quantum version of unique ergodicity for PSL_2(Z)\PSL_2(R)/K_\infty that has a significant implication: it suggests there are no exceptional Hecke-Siegel zeros. A major conjecture by Langlands posits that this quantum unique ergodicity hypothesis is equivalent to his broader conjecture about the absence of exceptional zeros. Both of these ideas will be shown to be quantum analogs of each other in a classical setting. Additionally, we propose a refined quantum unique ergodicity hypothesis with less stringent delocalization requirements, which would make it possible to prove there are no exceptional Hecke-Siegel zeros or demonstrate that Landau-Siegel zeros grow slowly in comparison to the critical line. A conjecture about this is put forward.

We enhance the quantum relational Hoare reasoning framework of de Haan and Kuntz with "expectations," enabling the expression of general pre and post conditions that capture program behavior in relation to each other. Much like their classical counterparts, quantum relational hoare triples take on the form of triples consisting of a precondition, a statement and a post condition. We define these triples such that they incorporate Gradual Type Checking, ensure the preservation of types across statements, and result in standard post conditions when they match the specified precondition. We demonstrate the application of this framework by deriving standard single-program correctness rules, including those for statement sequencing, conditional statements, and iterative loops.

The majority of disease transmission during an outbreak results from a small number of highly infectious individual occurrences. These events, known as super-spreader events, have gained considerable interest lately due to their influence on the spread of viruses like SARS-CoV-2. In order to include the effects of super-spreader events in models of epidemic growth, we develop and analyze a new stochastic model and discover the following key points: Absence of $R_0$ variability is insufficient to account for super-spreader events. Incorporating heavy-tailed distributions of individual infection counts provides a more comprehensive explanation. Our proposed model can be calibrated using data from the early stages of epidemics at the population level, and it leads to new methods for inferring the distribution of $R_0$. In addition to its relevance to epidemics, this has broader implications for other phenomena driven by the spread of viruses and cancers.

We also demonstrate a conic version of the cyclic set of operators, denoted as $Pol_+( \Omega)$, which provides a connection between Hirschowitz' work on moving squares and Swartz and Vasudeva's work on the moving circles. The study investigates the presence of bias in inferred vector magnetic field data, specifically in the Bz component, for objects such as sunspots and active regions. It aims to identify the sources of bias in measurement techniques used in this field. A comparative analysis is conducted between two common methods: spectropolarimetric inversion of the Ca II H line and indirect reconstruction from magnetograms. This analysis involves a computational experiment using synthetic data derived from 20 selected regions, encompassing individual pixels and entire region masks. Findings suggest that the CSH method introduces bias in both the Bz component and the total magnetic field, with the latter often exceeding the typical 50 Gauss limit for plausible PA line signals. However, by integrating direct measurements of the field perpendicular to the line of sight, this bias can be effectively reduced. In computational simulations, this adjustment results in a significant decrease in the mean absolute error from 178.58 Gauss to 50.18 Gauss for the Bz component. This represents a reduction in average absolute error of approximately 72%. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of measurement errors in vector magnetic field analysis, which is crucial for the accurate study of the structure and evolution of magnetic field configurations on the surface of the Sun.

Diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) simulations, a a hallmark of precise many-body physics calculations, are limited in their applicability to exotic and interesting cases due to a sign problem that arises in fermionic systems. This sign problem causes DMC estimates to lose precision as system size and simulation time increase, limiting its usefulness. We propose a potential solution to this problem by suggesting the use of complex-valued fully neural network wavefunctions to represent few-body dynamics. This approach significantly reduces the sign problem encountered in systems with multiple copies, enabling more than 100 DMC time steps to be completed while maintaining an effective variance of 1. With this method, we were able to accurately recreate the exact DMC estimate of the collisional loss rate for a two-dimensional Fermi gas near unitarity, a problem that previously could not be solved using the Laplacian Monte Carlo approach due to an inescapable sign problem. This suggests that multiple-copy systems, which were once considered hopeless due to the sign problem, may now be accessible to simulation using this proposed technique.

This study investigates how topological entropy and factor complexity change under free group basis transformations and homomorphisms. We establish that both metrics satisfy specific sub-additive properties: $\bar{s}(w) \bar{s}(v) \leq \bar{s}(wv)$ and $h(\Gamma) \geq h(\Lambda)$, indicating that the complexity of a word or a subgroup can vary depending on the chosen free group basis. However, for any reduced word $w$ with $s(w) > 0$ and initially for any subgroup $ \Lambda$ with $h(\Lambda) \geq 0$, there exists a reduction $w'$ equivalent to $w^{n}$ such that $s(w') \geq \frac{s(w)}{K} \geq s$ for some constant $K \geq 1$. Similarly, for the same conditions, there exists a subgroup $\Lambda'$ within the generated group that is isomorphic to $\Lambda$ and maintains the same factor complexity for words of a given length. We also provide necessary and sufficient conditions for $s(w)$ and $\Lambda$ to equal specific values.

This paper explores the creation of unsupervised cross-task generalization models to address costs and data scarcity associated with training controllers for new tasks. Tasks with high similarity can leverage pre-trained policies, but adding entirely new tasks requires relabeling and retraining, incurring significant expenses. We introduce a unsupervised cross-task generalization framework that enables tasks to utilize existing labels and untaged tasks to utilize no labels at all. We develop a two-stage approach consisting of a Variational Retrieval Enhancement model to capture latent features and a Retriental Augmentation stage that utilizes three modules - Knowledge Infusion, Prioritization, and Retriental Augmentation - to prioritize labeled data and integrate unlabeled tasks. Experiments show our method reduces training label requirements while outperforming benchmarks, demonstrating its practicality and efficiency in real-world settings.

This research focuses on identifying the Galois connections that define the structure of a specific group of matrix functions, specifically those comprising 2x2 inverse matrices over commutative rings. By characterizing these functions as ascending and descending operators within the set of matrix functions over these rings, we have a more concrete understanding of how this group of matrix functions is formed. Furthermore, for commutative fields with at least five distinct elements, we have established that the collection of these matrix functions forms a simple structure, specifically a minimal set. However, if these fields have between three and four elements, we have discovered that this collection of matrix functions constitutes a minimal ideal.

A novel statistical approach, called a two-method model, is applied to determine the properties of galaxies, building on previous success with star formations. In this study, it is shown that the model effectively characterizes APOGEE-2 galactic chemistry, linking age and metallicity patterns to different galactic components. By analyzing two methods of estimating metallicity ($\text{Zp}$), we find that $\text{Zp}$ is directly related to the age of stars in both inner and outer regions of the galaxy. Specifically, we observe an anti-correlation between metallicity and age for old populations in both areas. In addition, a new diagram is identified in the middle of the galaxy that is composed of intermediate metallicity populations. Using a simple model of the galaxy, we are able to fit the observed metallicity distributions and estimate the metallicity of each population. Furthermore, we find that the position of populations on this diagram is correlated with the local surface brightness of the galaxy. By analyzing the slopes of these relationships, we gain insight into the history of star formations in different areas of the Apogee region of the Milky Way. A new graph model called the spread tree has been introduced to analyze the dynamics of a viral video on Sina Weibo, which platform also facilitates a secondary propagation process. This spread tree consists of two primary components, primary nodes representing users who have posted the viral video, and secondary nodes denoting the associated connections of these users. This model's key advantage lies in its ability to identify influential primary nodes that have the potential to accelerate the propagation process. To identify these nodes, a optimized Monte Carlo method called the spread spread is utilized, which is then applied to a viral video on Sina Weibo during the COVID-19 pandemic. The resulting analysis reveals 10 highly influential nodes that have the potential to contribute to the rapid propagation of COVID-19 rumors.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxy clusters via extragalactic planetary nebulae has gained traction in recent years. To execute this method, researchers require comprehensive data on individual stellar nuclei from galaxy images to determine the H-alpha luminosity of each nebula, along with an independent way to calculate the H-alpha diameter of each stellar nucleus. In a recent study of the Hubble Deep Field South, Szomoru and Combes estimated the distance to the galaxy cluster by comparing the results with other measurement techniques. To apply this approach to the Fornax cluster, our primary objective is to identify all planetary nebulae within its galaxies. In a comprehensive analysis, we used the VLA's FSNS survey of the Fornax cluster to create a new inventory of planetary nebulae, examining nine different galaxies. In doing so, we calculated the radius of each planetary nebula using the major and minor axes of its structure as observed in radio spectra. Using the N2 ratio, we then estimated the surface brightness correction, the ionized gas mass, and the electron temperature of each planetary nebula. From this data, we calculated the distance to the Fornax cluster, obtaining a result of 19.9 Mpc with some margin of error. This estimate is consistent with other estimates based on planetary nebulae and matches the accepted value of the distance to the Fornax cluster within the same range of error.
